The following interactive figure will help us explore singular values and vectors geometrically before we begin a more algebraic approach.

Singular values, right singular vectors and left singular vectors

Select the matrix $A=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \amp 2 \\ -2 \amp - 1 \\ \end{bmatrix}$. As we vary the vector $\xvec$, we see the vector $A\xvec$ on the right in gray while the height of the blue bar to the right tells us $l_A(\xvec) = |A\xvec|$.

The first singular value $\sigma_1$ is the maximum value of $l_A(\xvec)$ over all unit vectors and an associated right singular vector $\vvec_1$ is a unit vector describing a direction in which this maximum occurs.

Use the diagram to find the first singular value $\sigma_1$ and an associated right singular vector $\vvec_1$.

The second singular value $\sigma_2$ is the minimum value of $l_A(\xvec)$ over all unit vectors and an associated right singular vector $\vvec_2$ is a unit vector describing a direction in which this minimum occurs.

Use the diagram to find the second singular value $\sigma_2$ and an associated right singular vector $\vvec_2$.

Here's how we can find the right singular values and vectors without using the diagram. Remember that $l_A(\xvec) = \sqrt{q_G(\xvec)}$ where $G=A^TA$ is the Gram matrix associated to $A$. Since $G$ is symmetric, it is orthogonally diagonalizable. Find $G$ and an orthogonal diagonalization of it.

What is the maximum value of the quadratic form $q_G(\xvec)$ among all unit vectors and in which direction does it occur? What is the minimum value of $q_G(\xvec)$ and in which direction does it occur?

Because $l_A(\xvec) = \sqrt{q_G(\xvec)}$, the first singular value $\sigma_1$ will be the square root of the maximum value of $q_G(\xvec)$ and $\sigma_2$ the square root of the minimum. Verify that the singular values that you found from the diagram are the square roots of the maximum and minimum values of $q_G(\xvec)$.

Verify that the right singular vectors $\vvec_1$ and $\vvec_2$ that you found from the diagram are the directions in which the maximum and minimum values occur.

Finally, we introduce the left singular vectors $\uvec_1$ and $\uvec_2$ by requiring that $A\vvec_1 = \sigma_1\uvec_1$ and $A\vvec_2=\sigma_2\uvec_2$. Find the two left singular vectors.

Form the matrices $$ U = \begin{bmatrix}\uvec_1 \amp \uvec_2 \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} \Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} \sigma_1 \amp 0 \\ 0 \amp \sigma_2 \\ \end{bmatrix}, \hspace{24pt} V = \begin{bmatrix}\vvec_1 \amp \vvec_2 \end{bmatrix} $$ and explain why $AV = U\Sigma$.

Finally, explain why $A=U\Sigma V^T$ and verify that this relationship holds for this specific example.
